name: Great Andamanese (Jeru)
script: Devanagari and IPA (documented by Anvita Abbi)
lead: Present-day Great Andamanese (based primarily on Aka-Jeru, with lexical elements from Khora, Sare, and Bo) is a Critically Endangered language spoken on Strait Island in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, India.[1][2] Documented extensively by Anvita Abbi between 2001 and 2013, the language is typologically notable for its obligatory somatic (body-division) prefixation system across nouns, verbs, and adjectives.[1][2]
history:
Prior to the establishment of the British penal colony in 1858, ten distinct Great Andamanese languages formed a dialect continuum from North to South Andaman.[1] Epidemic diseases and demographic collapse reduced the population from an estimated 5,000 in 1858 to 19 individuals by 1961.[1] In 1970, the Indian administration relocated the surviving community to Strait Island.[1]

The last speaker of the Bo variety (Boa Sr.) died in January 2010, and the last fluent speaker of the Jeru/Khora koiné, Licho, died in April 2020, leaving a handful of semi-speakers whose heritage is preserved in the Endangered Languages Archive (ELAR).[3]
phonology: Great Andamanese has a seven-vowel system (/i, e, ɛ, a, ɔ, o, u/) and a consonant inventory featuring bilabial, dental, alveolar, retroflex, palatal, and velar stops, including a bilabial fricative /ɸ/ and palatal/velar nasals /ɲ, ŋ/.[1][2]
syntax: A defining grammatical feature of Great Andamanese is its seven-zone somatic body-division prefix system: inalienable body parts, relational nouns, adjectives, and transitive verbs must carry a proclitic marker specifying which somatic zone is involved (e.g., er- for head/eyes/upper body, ut-/ot- for neck/round parts, oŋ- for hands/feet/extremities, a- for mouth/origin).[1][2]

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Pronominal Proclitics & Body-Zone Prefixes
lessons.intro: Possessor proclitics combine directly with somatic zone prefixes before nominal and verbal stems (Abbi 2013: 68–95).<sup>[2]</sup>

vocab.gloss: Class 2 somatic prefix (head, face, upper external body)

quiz.q: Which somatic prefix attaches to nouns associated with the hands, feet, and extremities?

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Inalienable Body Terms & Ecology
lessons.intro: Body-part nouns cited with first-person singular possessor t- + somatic class marker (Abbi 2012).<sup>[1]</sup>

quiz.q: Deconstruct the morphological structure of t-er-ulu ('my eye').
quiz.a: t- (1SG possessor) + er- (Class 2 upper-body somatic zone prefix) + ulu ('eye').

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Verbs & Tense-Aspect-Mood Suffixes
lessons.intro: Verbal roots and TAM suffixes from Abbi (2013: 185–210).<sup>[2]</sup>

quiz.q: Which suffix marks past/completive aspect on Great Andamanese verbs?
Why does the adjective bùng ('good/beautiful') carry the prefix er-?
quiz.a: Descriptive predicates take somatic zone prefixes indexing the external appearance or body part of the referent.
